note: corners are [RA_deg, Dec_deg] in JPEG raster order: TL, TR, BR, BL

images.label: NGC 55 Whale / Pearls
images.distance_note: Tip of the red giant branch; Karachentsev et al. 2003
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop

images.label: M31 Andromeda Galaxy
images.distance_note: About 765 kpc, commonly quoted as 2.5 million light-years.
images.discovered_by: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, 964
images.description:
The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest large spiral to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away, and the biggest member of our Local Group. Its light left before modern humans existed. Two of its satellite galaxies are in the frame: the compact M32 just off the disc, and the elongated M110 further out. NGC 206, a huge cloud of young blue stars, shows as a bright knot inside the outer spiral arm. From the southern hemisphere Andromeda sits low in the north, so it has to be caught in the short window when it clears the horizon murk.

This wide view brings several overlapping photographs together to show the galaxy and its neighbours in one frame.

images.label: NGC 253 Sculptor Galaxy
images.distance_note: Tip of the red giant branch; Radburn-Smith et al. 2011
images.discovered_by: Caroline Herschel

images.label: NGC 253 Sculptor (wide field)
images.distance_note: ~3.5–3.7 Mpc: Rekola et al. 2005 PNLF 3.34 Mpc; TRGB 3.7–3.94 Mpc (Karachentsev et al. 2003; Anand et al. 2021 3.70 Mpc). Range 3.34–3.94 Mpc; TRGB best regarded
images.discovered_by: Caroline Herschel, 1783. Conventional credit: Caroline Herschel
images.description:
The wide view brings two very different objects together. The long streak is NGC 253, a nearby galaxy with a busy centre where new stars are forming. The small, round gathering of stars is NGC 288, a globular cluster that belongs to the Milky Way.

Dark lanes cutting across the streak are dust in the galaxy, while the round cluster is made of old stars held together by gravity. The two appear close because we see them in the same direction, not because they are neighbours. The cluster is hundreds of times closer to Earth than the galaxy behind it.

images.label: NGC 292 Small Magellanic Cloud
images.distance_note: Graczyk et al. 2020, ApJ 904, 13, D=62.44±0.47(stat)±0.81(syst) kpc (late-type eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: Naked-eye object known since antiquity; first European written record by members of Magellan's expedition, 1519. No individual discovery credit
images.description:
The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy and one of the Milky Way's prominent neighbours in the southern sky. Its irregular outline is a contrast to the tidy arms of a spiral galaxy. Gravity from its encounters with the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way has helped shape it.

The cloud also has fewer heavy elements than the Milky Way, giving astronomers a nearby place to study how stars form in a different chemical environment. Within the broad glow, bright knots trace pockets of recent star formation, while diffuse light comes from many stars blending together at this distance.

images.label: NGC 346 (SMC)
images.distance_note: Host galaxy SMC: Graczyk et al. 2020, ApJ 904, 13, 62.44 kpc (eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834–36 (Cape of Good Hope survey); catalogued in Dreyer's NGC 1888. Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 346 is a young star cluster and one of the busiest stellar nurseries in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a companion galaxy to the Milky Way. The hot young stars light up the surrounding gas, while denser lanes of gas and dust provide material for stars still forming.

Ridges and arcs help make the boundaries between those regions visible. The Small Magellanic Cloud contains relatively little of the heavier elements that astronomers call metals. That makes NGC 346 a useful nearby comparison for how stars formed in the early universe, when those elements were also less abundant.

images.label: SMC core, NGC 346 region (HOO)
images.distance_note: Host galaxy SMC: Graczyk et al. 2020, ApJ 904, 13, 62.44 kpc (eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834–36 (Cape survey); NGC 1888
images.description:
The Small Magellanic Cloud is a neighbouring galaxy about 200,000 light-years away. Around its young star cluster NGC 346, radiation energises the surrounding gas and makes it shine. This view draws attention to the light from hydrogen and oxygen, so the curved rims and thin strands of glowing gas stand out among the stars.

The shapes record how successive generations of massive stars have disturbed the cloud around them. It is a view of one small part of a galaxy, but also a good example of how stars can reshape the places where they were born.

images.label: NGC 460 (N84)
images.distance_note: Host galaxy SMC: Graczyk et al. 2020, ApJ 904, 13, 62.44 kpc (eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 11 April 1834 (Cape survey); possibly seen earlier by James Dunlop, 1826
images.description: NGC 460 is an open cluster wrapped in glowing hydrogen gas in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy about 200,000 light-years away in the constellation Tucana. Its nebula carries the Henize catalogue number N84, and it sits next to its neighbour NGC 456 in the N83-84-85 complex, a region of linked clusters and nebulae that is home to several rare O-type stars, the hottest and most massive normal stars there are. The stars here are only one to ten million years old. Their radiation ionises the surrounding hydrogen so it glows, while their winds and radiation blow the gas into bubbles and shells, and that compression can set off a new round of star formation. The Small Magellanic Cloud also has fewer heavy elements than the Milky Way, so it is a close-up look at star formation under conditions more like those of the early universe.

images.label: NGC 474 Shell Galaxy
images.distance_note: Surface brightness fluctuation; ~32 Mpc. Estimates range 95-110 Mly
images.discovered_by: William Herschel
images.description:
At first, NGC 474 looks like a smooth, oval galaxy. Look again outside the bright core and you can make out a series of pale arcs, like ripples spreading away from the centre. These shells are made of stars rather than gas. They are among the clearest clues that the galaxy has absorbed smaller neighbours.

As a smaller galaxy is pulled apart, its stars keep moving on related paths. They can bunch up where they slow near the far ends of their orbits, making the shells stand out. The faint edges are a record of past mergers that the bright centre alone would not reveal.

images.label: M74 Phantom Galaxy
images.distance_note: About 30 million light-years (published estimates typically 24–32 million ly).
images.discovered_by: Pierre Méchain, 1780
images.description: M 74, the Phantom Galaxy, is a face-on grand design spiral in Pisces, about 30 million light-years away. Its two clean spiral arms are packed with young blue stars, and the pink knots along them are clouds of glowing hydrogen lit by newborn stars. It fills only a quarter of this frame, set among faint background galaxies.

images.label: NGC 1097
images.distance_note: Commonly quoted value (ESO/ALMA). Redshift distances are typically 14–18 Mpc (about 46–59 million ly); Galianni et al. 2010 adopted 17 ± 2 Mpc.
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1790
images.description:
NGC 1097 is a barred spiral galaxy about 45 million light-years away in Fornax. A bright bar of stars cuts across its core and funnels gas inward, feeding a ring of star formation about 5,000 light-years across. At the heart sits a supermassive black hole about 140 million times the mass of the Sun. The small yellow glow at the upper right is the dwarf companion NGC 1097A.

Those features once called jets are four faint, narrow streams of stars, radiating in an X from the galaxy. They are not jets from the black hole: they are tidal debris, the remains of a dwarf galaxy that NGC 1097 has been tearing apart. The brightest of them, R1, runs northeast and bends at a right angle — the “dog-leg” — about 13 arcminutes out. A faint linear glow in the upper left of this frame follows the path of that stream.

images.label: Comet 220P McNaught
images.constellation: Aries (transient — a comet's constellation changes with time and depends on the imaging epoch)
images.distance_note: Not applicable — Solar System body; light-year distance is not meaningful. Orbital elements (JPL/MPC): Jupiter-family comet in near-2:1 resonance with Jupiter, period ~5.5 yr, perihelion q≈1.6 AU (perihelion 14 June 2026), aphelion 4.679 AU (reached 12 March 2029)
images.discovered_by: Robert H. McNaught, 20 May 2004 (Siding Spring Survey, Uppsala Southern Schmidt Telescope, Siding Spring Observatory, NSW); announced as P/2004 K2 in IAU Circular 8348 (28 May 2004), confirmed by J. Young and A. Gilmore. Conventional credit: McNaught
images.description:
220P/McNaught is a short-period comet discovered by Robert McNaught at Siding Spring in New South Wales. Its solid nucleus is small compared with the surrounding coma, the diffuse cloud that forms when sunlight warms the ice and gas escapes, carrying dust with it.

A green tint in a comet's coma can come from carbon molecules fluorescing in sunlight. Look for the change from a bright centre to a softer envelope, rather than expecting the nucleus itself to be resolved. Unlike the stars behind it, a comet can noticeably change position from one night to the next as it moves around the Sun.

images.label: NGC 1365 Great Barred Spiral
images.distance_note: ~18.1–18.6 Mpc: Hoyt et al. 2021 TRGB 18.1±0.5 Mpc; Madore et al./Silbermann et al. 1999 Cepheid 18.6±0.6 Mpc (Fornax Cluster). Midpoint ~18.3 Mpc; TRGB and Cepheid determinations agree
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826 (Parramatta, NSW). Conventional credit: Dunlop
images.description:
NGC 1365 is a barred spiral in the Fornax Cluster. Its straight central bar and sweeping arms make an especially clear example of the way spiral galaxies can be organised. The bar is a pattern made of orbiting stars, not a rigid structure, and its gravity can steer gas towards the galaxy's centre.

Some of that gas feeds star formation in the inner region. The central black hole is also active. The contrast between the straight bar, the curved arms and the clumpy places where new stars are forming gives a sense of how different parts of a galaxy can evolve together.

images.label: NGC 1433
images.distance_note: About 50 million light-years, the figure used in coverage of SN 2026ahvu. Published distance estimates are typically around 46 million ly (14.15 ± 1.15 Mpc).
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826
images.description: NGC 1433 is a barred spiral galaxy in Horologium, about 50 million light-years away. The bluish star just above and to the right of the core, on the inner ring, is supernova SN 2026ahvu, a Type Ia explosion discovered on 2 November 2026. James Dunlop found the galaxy in 1826 from Parramatta.

images.label: M45 Pleiades
images.distance_note: 136.2 pc from VLBI parallax; Melis et al. 2014, resolving the long-running disagreement with the Hipparcos value
images.discovered_by: Known since antiquity
images.description:
The Pleiades are a family of young stars in Taurus, close enough for the brightest members to make a little cluster visible to the naked eye. A longer look shows something the eye usually misses: delicate blue wisps around the stars, with some strands looking almost brushed across the sky.

The wisps are dust, not gas glowing on its own. The cluster is passing through a cloud, and starlight scattered by its dust grains reaches us as a blue haze. The bright stars and the cloud look like one object here, but they are two things briefly sharing the same space.

images.label: NGC 1532
images.distance_note: About 55 million light-years (published estimates typically 55–58 million ly; NED 58.3 ± 1.5 million ly).
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826
images.description: NGC 1532, also known as Haley's Coronet, is a barred spiral galaxy in Eridanus, seen edge-on, about 55 million light-years away. It is locked in a slow gravitational dance with the dwarf galaxy NGC 1531, the small yellowish glow just below the core. Tidal forces have lifted part of the disc and drawn a bridge of gas and dust between the pair. The faint elongated galaxy at the upper right is ESO 359-G29.

images.label: IC 2118 Witch Head
images.distance_note: ~210 pc (Kun et al. 2001); the illuminating star Rigel/β Orionis lies ~264 pc (Hipparcos/Gaia). Popular ~900 ly is a rough figure
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1786 (bright portion = NGC 1909); IC 2118 designation in Dreyer's Index Catalogue 1895. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
This cloud in Eridanus has the sharp nose and chin of a face in profile. It doesn’t shine like a star or glow like the gas in many nebulae. Its light comes from Rigel, the bright blue star in Orion, which illuminates it from the side.

The blue is a clue: fine dust scatters shorter wavelengths of light more readily than longer ones. In other words, we see Rigel by reflection, even though the star itself is not the subject of the photograph. The same effect lets us trace a cloud that would otherwise be hard to see.

images.label: NGC 2018 (LMC)
images.distance_note: Host galaxy LMC: Pietrzyński et al. 2019, Nature 567, 200, 49.59±0.09(stat)±0.54(syst) kpc (eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834–36 (Cape survey); NGC 1888
images.description:
NGC 2018 lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. The red glow marks hydrogen gas lit by hot young stars. At first glance it looks like a soft wash of colour, but follow the brighter rims and you can see where the light picks out the edges of clouds.

The rounded blue-green bubble nearby offers a different view of what massive stars can do. Their winds can clear space around them and pile up gas into a shell. What looks like a neat ring from Earth is the bright edge of a much larger structure.

images.label: M1 Crab Nebula
images.discovered_by: John Bevis, 1731. The supernova itself was recorded by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1054
images.distance_note: ~2.0 kpc, conventional. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
The Crab Nebula is what remains of a star whose explosion was recorded in 1054. For a time the new point of light could be seen even in daylight. Today, the outer strands in the picture trace gas flung outward by that blast, still expanding centuries after the event.

There is a second source of energy at work inside. The collapsed core is a pulsar, a neutron star that spins about thirty times every second. It drives a wind of charged particles that lights the smoother interior. The photograph shows both the debris of the explosion and the continuing influence of the star it left behind.

images.label: NGC 2070 Tarantula Nebula
images.distance_note: Host galaxy LMC: Pietrzyński et al. 2019, Nature 567, 200, 49.59 kpc (eclipsing binaries)
images.discovered_by: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, 1751–52 (Cape; originally catalogued as the 'star' 30 Doradus); NGC number from Dreyer 1888. Conventional credit: Lacaille
images.description:
The Tarantula Nebula lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, outside the Milky Way. Even from that distance it stands out as one of the great stellar nurseries of the Local Group. The curved ridges of light outline cavities in the cloud, where the youngest, hottest stars are blowing gas out of their surroundings.

At the heart of the nebula is R136, a tight cluster that contains some of the most massive stars known. Several weigh more than a hundred Suns. They burn their fuel quickly, so the nebula lets us see a particularly short, energetic stage in the life of stars.

images.label: IC 434 Horsehead Nebula
images.discovered_by: Williamina Fleming, 1888, from a Harvard photographic plate
images.distance_note: ~400 pc to the L1630 / Orion B cloud (Gaia-era). Popularly quoted as 1,500 ly. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
The Horsehead is a dark cloud in Orion outlined against the glow of IC 434. The bright gas behind it and the dusty silhouette in front are two different features; the darker shape does not emit less light simply because it is farther away.

Dense dust absorbs the background glow, picking out the familiar muzzle and neck. Ultraviolet light from the Sigma Orionis system illuminates and slowly erodes the cloud’s surface. The sharp outline offers a way to see where unusually dense material has survived while the more exposed gas around it has been worn away.

images.label: Henize 70
images.distance_note: LMC distance, 49.6 kpc (about 162,000 ly), from eclipsing binaries; Pietrzyński et al. 2019. Henize 70 is taken to sit at the LMC's distance
images.discovered_by: Karl Henize (catalogued 1956)
images.description: Henize 70 is a superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud: a near-circular shell of glowing gas about 340 light-years across. Ultraviolet light from the hot, massive stars of the young association LH 114 ionises the gas, with shocks adding to the glow, and the stars' winds have been inflating the shell, which is still expanding at about 60 to 70 kilometres per second. The gas inside is heated to millions of degrees and shines in X-rays, brighter than winds alone should manage, which points to a recent supernova inside as well. It is a close-up look at how clusters of massive stars stir up and shape their host galaxy, though just what energised this one is still debated.

images.label: M78 (NGC 2068)
images.distance_note: Commonly quoted value, about 400–420 pc to the Orion B molecular cloud.
images.discovered_by: Pierre Méchain, 1780
images.description: M 78 is one of the brightest reflection nebulae in the sky, about 1,350 light-years away in Orion. It makes no light of its own: two young, hot B-type stars at its heart, HD 38563 A and B, scatter their blue-white light off a cloud of fine dust. This wide view shows the bright blue-white core threaded with near-black dust lanes, a dark spiky cloud off to the upper right, and a pink glow of hydrogen along the left edge. It is my first finished image from the Nebula Nest.

images.label: NGC 2174 Monkey Head Nebula
images.discovered_by: Karl Christian Bruhns, 1857
images.distance_note: ~2.0 kpc, conventional. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
The Monkey Head Nebula in Orion is a place where stars are still forming. The intense light of young stars makes the surrounding gas glow and wears away the surface of the cloud. Look for the darker knots and pillars in the brighter gas.

They are denser regions that can hold out longer against the radiation and may shelter young stars we cannot see in visible light. Infrared observations can reveal some of those hidden stars. The nickname comes from the outline, but the small structures along its edges tell the more interesting story.

images.label: NGC 2237 Rosette Nebula
images.discovered_by: Nebulosity: Lewis Swift, 1865 (NGC 2237). The central cluster NGC 2244 was seen by John Flamsteed around 1690
images.distance_note: ~1.6 kpc, conventional. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
The Rosette is a broad cloud of glowing gas in Monoceros, with the young open cluster NGC 2244 at its heart. The ring of brighter material outlines a cavity carved by the cluster’s hottest stars. Their winds help clear gas from the centre, and their ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow.

Dense fingers and knots around the rim have resisted erosion longer than the thinner material around them. The flower-like outline is striking, but this is a three-dimensional cloud: the bright rim is partly a consequence of looking through its thicker edges.

images.label: NGC 2264 Cone Nebula
images.distance_note: ~719–738 pc: Maíz Apellániz 2019 (Gaia DR2) 719±16 pc; Kuhn et al. 2019 738 pc (Mon OB1)
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1785 (Cone Nebula, H V.27); associated cluster 1784. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
The Cone Nebula is a pillar of relatively dense gas and dust in NGC 2264, a star-forming region in Monoceros that also contains the Christmas Tree Cluster. Hot young stars illuminate the cloud and erode the less protected gas around it.

The cone persists because denser material resists that erosion longer than its surroundings. Its dark interior and the bright outlines of exposed gas are useful clues: one blocks light from behind, while the other is being lit from outside. What looks like a solid peak is really a cloud with a long, slow process of erosion under way.

images.label: Sh2-308 Dolphin Head
images.distance_note: Distance to central star WR 6/EZ CMa (HD 50896) uncertain: Rate & Crowther 2020 (Gaia DR2) ~2.27 kpc (~7,400 ly); Gaia DR3 reductions ~1,537 pc (~5,010 ly); older 1,389–1,800 pc (4,530–5,870 ly), Hipparcos-2007 ~1,400 pc. Value shown ~1,900 pc is a midpoint of Gaia-era estimates; genuinely uncertain
images.discovered_by: Stewart Sharpless, 1959 (Sharpless catalogue Sh2-308; = RCW 11, LBN 1052)
images.description:
The Dolphin Head is a bubble around EZ Canis Majoris, an evolved Wolf–Rayet star in Canis Major. A fast wind from the star has pushed into older material around it, piling gas into a thin, expanding shell.

The outline can look brighter along the rim because our view passes through more of the emitting shell there than it does looking straight through the middle. Light from doubly ionised oxygen is especially conspicuous in parts of this nebula. The sharp curves are the boundaries of a stellar wind at work, not the wreckage of a supernova.

images.label: IC 2177 Seagull Nebula
images.distance_note: ~1,120 pc via the ionising Be star HD 53367 (Gaia); commonly cited ~3,800 ly. NOTE: the supplied centre coordinate (Dec −11.11°) falls within Canis Major by IAU (Delporte 1930) boundaries, though the nebula straddles the Monoceros border
images.discovered_by: Isaac Roberts, 1898 (photographic); IC 2177 in Dreyer's Index Catalogue 1910. Conventional credit: Roberts
images.description:
The Seagull is a sprawling complex of glowing gas near the boundary of Monoceros and Canis Major. Its rounded head is known as Sharpless 2-292, while the much larger arcs that suggest wings are part of Sharpless 2-296.

The bright star HD 53367 helps light the gas in the head; ultraviolet light from hot stars ionises hydrogen, which then gives off light. The bird is a nickname for the arrangement of these separate structures in the sky. Following the wing-like arcs is a good way to appreciate how much farther the complex extends beyond its brightest patch.

images.label: NGC 2359 Thor's Helmet
images.distance_note: Conventional ~3,670 pc (~11,960 ly). The Gaia DR2 parallax of WR 7/HD 56925 (0.210±0.027 mas) is low-precision (~15% error) and variously interpreted (implying ~4,800 pc); no consensus downward revision. Distance uncertain
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1785. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
Thor's Helmet is an emission nebula in Canis Major with a rounded shell and long extensions that suggest the wings of a helmet. Its sculptor is WR 7, a hot, evolved Wolf–Rayet star that is shedding material in a fast stellar wind.

As that wind runs into slower gas around the star, it sweeps the gas into a shell. The bubble is expanding into a patchy neighbourhood, which helps explain why it is neither smooth nor symmetrical. The round part and the irregular extensions are two ways to see what happens when a powerful wind meets uneven material.

images.label: NGC 2467 Skull and Crossbones
images.distance_note: Line-of-sight superposition — no single distance. HII region S311 ionised by O6 star HD 64315 (~4.1 kpc); superposed unrelated clusters Haffner 18 ~4.5 kpc (~14,700 ly) and Haffner 19 ~6.4 kpc (~20,900 ly), Vázquez et al. 2010. Value shown is for the S311/Haffner 18 component
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1784. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 2467 is a busy star-forming region in Puppis, nicknamed the Skull and Crossbones for its bright and dark shapes. Hot young stars light up the gas around them, while denser clumps of dust and gas stand in front of the glow like silhouettes.

Some look like pillars because the exposed material around them has been worn away more quickly. The stars and clouds we see in this direction are not all at the same distance. The image is a useful reminder that a single striking shape on the sky can combine several layers along our line of sight.

images.label: Vela Supernova Remnant
images.distance_note: 287 pc (~936 ly) from Vela pulsar VLBI parallax 3.5±0.2 mas, Dodson et al. 2003, ApJ 596, 1137; cf. HST optical parallax 294 pc (Caraveo et al. 2001). Supersedes the older kinematic ~500 pc. Popular ~815 ly is too low
images.discovered_by: Vela pulsar (PSR B0833-45) discovered 1968 by Large, Vaughan & Mills (Molonglo, NSW); the SNR was mapped in 1950s–60s radio surveys. Conventional credit for the pulsar: Large et al. 1968
images.description:
The scattered arcs in Vela are debris from a star that exploded roughly 11,000 years ago. The blast has since spread over a region of sky many times wider than the full Moon. Its outlines are brightest where the expanding shock meets denser gas and heats it enough to shine.

The explosion also left a pulsar, the compact core of the star. It spins about eleven times a second; its beams can sweep past Earth like a lighthouse. The thin luminous threads and the tiny spinning remnant are very different traces of the same event.

images.label: NGC 2736 Pencil Nebula
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1835 (Cape of Good Hope survey)
images.distance_note: 287 pc, from the Vela pulsar VLBI parallax (Dodson et al.). Same value as the Vela SNR entry - the Pencil is part of it.
images.description:
The Pencil Nebula is a thin-looking piece of the much larger Vela supernova remnant. It is not a narrow rod floating in space: the bright line is the edge of a sheet of gas. We see it almost side-on, so light from more of the sheet is packed into a thin strip in our view.

The gas glows where it is heated by the shock from the explosion of a star around 11,000 years ago. Follow the bright edge and it starts to look less like a straight pencil and more like a folded ribbon.

images.label: NGC 3293 Gem Cluster
images.distance_note: ~2,335 pc (~7,600 ly): Dias et al. 2021 (Gaia DR2) 2,334±52 pc; Göppl & Preibisch 2022 (Gaia EDR3) ~2.3 kpc
images.discovered_by: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, 1751 (Cape; Lac). Conventional credit: Lacaille
images.description:
The Gem Cluster is a young open cluster in Carina, a group of stars born from the same molecular cloud. Its tight grouping is speckled with hot blue stars, making the contrast with its prominent reddish star especially striking. Blue stars generally have hotter surfaces than red ones, but colour alone is not a measure of age.

For a cluster whose members formed around the same time, the differences tell us more about mass and how quickly stars change. The most massive stars use their fuel much faster than the Sun and can evolve while their lower-mass neighbours are still young.

images.label: NGC 3324 Gabriela Mistral
images.distance_note: ~2.3 kpc (~7,500 ly): Göppl & Preibisch 2022, Gaia EDR3 OB-star sample; adopted by the JWST Early Release Observations 2022. The popular ~9,100 ly (2,800 pc) is outdated
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826 (Parramatta, NSW). Conventional credit: Dunlop
images.description:
NGC 3324 is a young cluster in the Gum 31 nebula, near the northwestern edge of the Carina Nebula complex. Radiation from hot stars illuminates and erodes the edge of a dense cloud there, producing a ragged wall that has earned comparisons with both cliffs and a human profile.

The ridgeline marks a change between a more exposed region of glowing gas and the cloud's denser interior. The James Webb Space Telescope's Cosmic Cliffs view explores a portion of this boundary, where it revealed jets from young stars that are difficult to see in visible light.

images.label: NGC 3372 Carina Nebula
images.distance_note: 2.3 kpc (Smith 2006, expansion parallax of the η Carinae Homunculus)
images.discovered_by: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, 1751–52 (Cape). Conventional credit: Lacaille
images.description:
Carina is a vast nursery where hot young stars light up the gas they formed from. The bright clouds are broken by dark shapes, including the Keyhole. These are places where thicker dust blocks the light behind it. Along the edges, radiation and winds from nearby stars wear away the exposed material, leaving pillars and ridges.

The nebula also contains Eta Carinae, a massive pair of stars with a particularly turbulent history. In the 1840s it briefly became one of the brightest stars in the night sky. The material thrown off in that eruption still surrounds the pair.

images.label: IC 2631 Chamaeleon Complex
images.distance_note: 192.7±0.4 pc (~629 ly), Gaia DR2 parallaxes to the Chamaeleon I North cloud, 2018; older ~160 pc (Whittet et al. 1997)
images.discovered_by: DeLisle Stewart, 1900 (photographic; = Cederblad 112); IC designation in Dreyer's Index Catalogue
images.description:
IC 2631 is part of the Chamaeleon I cloud, one of the closer regions where new stars are forming. The diffuse blue glow is not produced by the dust itself: it is light from the young star HD 97300 scattered by the dust around it.

Where the material is thick enough, the same cloud can turn dark by blocking the light behind it. Look for the transitions between the blue glow and those darker patches. Both reveal the dusty surroundings of young stars, but they show them by opposite effects.

images.label: Gum 37 Tadpoles and Statue of Liberty (wide)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834-38 (Cape of Good Hope survey)
images.distance_note: ~2.35 kpc for NGC 3572 / Gum 37. NGC 3576 in the same frame is separately given as 9,100 ly, so this wide field spans both.
images.description:
This wide view brings together two parts of Carina's star-forming landscape: the tadpole-like streamers near NGC 3572 and the area of NGC 3576 nicknamed the Statue of Liberty. Both owe their glow to hot young stars, but the resulting shapes vary with the density and arrangement of the original clouds.

Narrow protrusions mark dense material that has resisted erosion, while more diffuse glow traces gas exposed to ultraviolet light. The two regions look close together in the sky; the wider perspective is useful for comparing their structures, not for assuming all the gas lies at the same distance from us.

images.label: NGC 3572 Gum 37 Southern Tadpoles
images.distance_note: ~2.0–2.7 kpc: SIMBAD/VizieR ~2.0 kpc; Steppe 1977 (RGU photometry) 2.7 kpc. Midpoint ~2.35 kpc (~7,600 ly); range 6,500–8,800 ly
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834 (Cape). Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
In Carina, the young star cluster NGC 3572 sits amid glowing gas threaded with narrow, tadpole-like clouds. The dense heads can shield material behind them while radiation and winds from hot stars wear away their more exposed sides.

The tails are clues to how the surrounding cloud is being sculpted, though individual shapes need not all point in a single direction. Look for the contrast between the compact knots and the much smoother glow of the surrounding gas. The knots are not simply decorations on the nebula: they mark places where denser material has survived longer.

images.label: NGC 3572 / Gum 37
images.distance_note: ~2.0–2.7 kpc: SIMBAD ~2.0 kpc; Steppe 1977 2.7 kpc. Midpoint ~2.35 kpc; range 6,500–8,800 ly
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834 (Cape). Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
Gum 37 is a cloud of glowing gas in Carina. A wider view makes it easier to see how the small, dark “tadpoles” fit into the cloud around NGC 3572. Look for the dense heads and the long tails trailing away from the young stars.

Their intense light heats and erodes the gas on the side that faces them, while the denser knots protect material behind them. The tails are a record of the direction the light is coming from, even though the cloud itself has no hard edge.

images.label: NGC 3576 Statue of Liberty
images.distance_note: ~2.4–3.0 kpc: Persi et al. 1994 ~2.4 kpc; Damineli et al. 2002 ~2.8 kpc. Value ~2.8 kpc (~9,100 ly)
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834 (Cape). Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
The Statue of Liberty Nebula is a stellar nursery in Carina, named for a shape some people see in its glowing gas. Its most striking structures are looping filaments. Young, massive stars hidden in the cloud drive winds that push into the surrounding material, helping carve the arcs and cavities.

The loops are easiest to follow where the gas is brightest, but the dark stretches between them are part of the pattern too. They help show how uneven a star-forming cloud can be, with dense pockets beside regions that have already been hollowed out.

images.label: NGC 3628 Hamburger Galaxy
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1784
images.distance_note: ~10.7 Mpc. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
NGC 3628 is a spiral galaxy in the Leo Triplet, alongside M65 and M66. It is seen almost edge-on, so its spiral arms are hard to distinguish and the dusty disc appears as a thick dark stripe across its starlight.

The edges of the disc flare and bend rather than forming a clean, straight line. That distortion, together with a much fainter tidal tail, is evidence of gravitational encounters in the group. The dust lane gives the galaxy its nickname; the warp is the feature that hints at its history.

images.label: IC 2944 Running Chicken
images.distance_note: ~2,331 pc (~7,600 ly), Gaia DR3 (Reipurth et al. 2025) to the OB subgroup; older popular ~6,500 ly (2,000 pc)
images.discovered_by: Nebula (IC 2944/2948): Royal H. Frost, 1904 (Bruce telescope, Arequipa); Thackeray's globules: A. D. Thackeray, 1950. Conventional credit for nebula: Frost
images.description:
The Running Chicken Nebula in Centaurus is a cloud of gas lit by young stars. Its nickname comes from a bird-like outline some observers see in the brighter material. Another detail worth looking for is the small dark shapes set against the glow.

These are dense knots of dust and gas, known as Thackeray’s Globules, seen in silhouette. The young stars nearby are steadily wearing away their surfaces with intense light. Some such knots can shelter developing stars, though it is not clear whether these particular ones will last long enough to do so.

images.label: NGC 4038 Antennae Galaxies
images.distance_note: 22±3 Mpc (Schweizer et al. 2008, AJ 136, 1482, from Type Ia SN 2007sr and a revised TRGB 20.0 Mpc, plus a flow model 22.5 Mpc). This supersedes the short 13.3 Mpc TRGB of Saviane et al. 2008, attributed to a TRGB misidentification. Best regarded: 22 Mpc
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1785. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
The Antennae are two spiral galaxies in Corvus in the middle of a merger. Their namesake tails are long arcs of stars and gas pulled out by gravity as the galaxies passed one another.

The tails and the bright concentrations at the hearts of the two galaxies tell different parts of the story: gravity rearranges the stars, while colliding clouds compress gas and spark new star formation. Individual stars are so far apart that direct collisions between them are rare. The encounter is dramatic on the scale of whole galaxies, not a pile-up of individual suns.

images.label: Sandqvist 149 Dark Doodad
images.distance_note: Musca molecular cloud from Gaia 3D dust: Zucker et al. 2021 ~171–173 pc; Musca filament ~140–150 pc (Franco 1991; Cox et al. 2016). Range ~140–190 pc; midpoint ~165 pc (~538 ly). Supersedes older ~700 ly figures
images.discovered_by: Aage Sandqvist, 1977 (Stockholm Observatory; dark-cloud catalogue, from ESO(B) Schmidt plates); nickname 'Dark Doodad' coined by Dennis di Cicco, 1986
images.description:
The Dark Doodad is a long, narrow streak through the star fields of Musca. It looks like a tear in the sky, but it is a cloud in front of the stars, not a gap between them. Fine grains of dust in the cold molecular gas block much of the visible light behind the filament.

The edges are useful clues: where the cloud thins, more background stars show through. Filaments like this are common in molecular clouds and can concentrate the gas from which stars form, although not every dark strand is actively making stars.

images.label: M104 Sombrero Galaxy
images.distance_note: 9.55±0.13(stat)±0.31(syst) Mpc (McQuinn et al. 2016, AJ 152, 144, HST TRGB); consistent with SBF ~9.1 Mpc
images.discovered_by: Pierre Méchain, 1781; added to Messier's catalogue (M104) later. Conventional credit: Méchain
images.description:
The Sombrero Galaxy in Virgo is easiest to recognise by its broad central glow and the remarkably sharp dark band across it. The band is not a separate object. It is the galaxy’s own dusty ring, seen almost edge-on and silhouetted against the starlight behind it.

The bright material above and below the band makes the central bulge look rounder than the thin disc around it. That combination of a prominent bulge and narrow disc is what gives M104 its hat-like profile, and it has made the galaxy an interesting case for classification.

images.label: NGC 5128 Centaurus A
images.distance_note: 3.8±0.1 Mpc (Harris, Rejkuba & Harris 2010, PASA 27, 457 — best-estimate mean of Cepheid, TRGB, PNLF, SBF and Mira methods)
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826 (Parramatta, NSW). Conventional credit: Dunlop
images.description:
Centaurus A is a galaxy with two very different faces. Its broad, pale body looks smooth, but a thick, ragged band of dust cuts across the middle. The dust and gas are evidence of a past merger. Look along the lane for the contrast between clouds blocking older starlight and brighter patches where new stars are forming.

The centre holds a supermassive black hole. Material falling towards it powers jets that reach far beyond the visible galaxy. Those jets show up especially well in radio and X-ray observations, so this picture in visible light tells only part of the story.

images.label: M83 Southern Pinwheel
images.distance_note: ~4.5–4.9 Mpc: Thim et al. 2003 Cepheid 4.5 Mpc (μ=28.32); Karachentsev et al. 2007 TRGB ~4.9 Mpc (μ=28.56). Midpoint ~4.6 Mpc
images.discovered_by: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille, 1752 (Cape); added to Messier's catalogue (M83) 1781. Conventional credit: Lacaille
images.description:
M83 is a nearby spiral galaxy in Hydra, seen close to face-on. That angle makes it easy to follow the arms as they curl away from the brighter central region. The arms are places where new stars are forming: hot young stars contribute blue light, while glowing clouds of hydrogen mark concentrated sites of star birth.

Dust can also trace darker lanes along the arms. The core’s warmer glow comes in part from older stars. Several supernovae have been observed in M83, another sign of how quickly some of its massive stars live and die.

images.label: NGC 5367 / CG 12
images.distance_note: ~630 pc (Williams et al. 1977); alternative ~550 pc (Maheswar et al.). No clean modern Gaia DR3 determination located; range ~550–630 pc. Value shown ~630 pc ≈ 2,050 ly. Amateur ~2,500 ly figures are not well supported
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834 (nebula NGC 5367); the cometary globule CG 12 was catalogued by Hawarden & Brand, 1976. Conventional credit for NGC 5367: J. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 5367 is the reflection nebula in the head of Cometary Globule 12, a cloud in Centaurus. The word cometary describes the rounded head and tapering tail, not an object in motion across the Solar System. In the bright head, dust scatters light from nearby young stars.

In denser stretches, dust instead shows up by blocking light from stars farther away. That switch from luminous haze to dark silhouette helps trace the shape of the cloud. The head and tail are parts of the same structure, but how the globule acquired its shape is less certain.

images.label: Barnard 228 Dark Wolf
images.distance_note: ~155 pc (~505 ly), Lupus 1 cloud: Galli et al. 2020 (Gaia DR2) 150–160 pc; Zucker et al. 2021 ~155 pc. Popular ~500 ly is coincidentally close
images.discovered_by: E. E. Barnard (Barnard Catalogue of 349 Dark Objects, published 1927). Conventional credit: Barnard
images.description:
Barnard 228 is a dark cloud in the nearby Lupus star-forming region. Its dust absorbs and scatters the light of stars behind it, so the cloud shows up more clearly by hiding things than by shining itself. The darkness isn't empty sky, and the occasional star that seems to sit within it may be on the near side.

The cloud belongs to a neighbourhood where pockets of cold gas can collapse to form new stars. At visible wavelengths, the contrast between star-rich fields and dark patches reveals where the material for those future stars lies.

images.label: IC 4601 Blue Reflection
images.distance_note: Part of the Rho Ophiuchi / Upper Scorpius complex; Gaia distances to the association cluster near 140 pc
images.discovered_by: Edward Emerson Barnard
images.description:
The delicate blue cloud belongs to the Rho Ophiuchi region, one of the nearest places where new stars are forming. Here, the colour comes from dust scattering light from nearby stars rather than from gas glowing on its own. Shorter, bluer wavelengths are scattered more readily, giving the cloud its cool colour.

Look for the contrast between the glow and the darker lanes. They can both be made of dust: a layer lit from the side is visible by reflected light, while thicker material hides the stars behind it. The photograph shows both effects in the same part of the sky.

images.label: LDN 1688 Rho Ophiuchi Complex
images.distance_note: 137.3±1.2 pc (~448 ly), Ortiz-León et al. 2017 (VLBA trigonometric parallaxes); confirmed by Gaia DR2 138.4±2.6 pc (Ortiz-León et al. 2018)
images.discovered_by: Beverly T. Lynds, 1962 (Lynds Dark Nebulae catalogue, from POSS plates). Conventional credit: Lynds
images.description:
The Rho Ophiuchi complex is a nearby region where new stars are forming in clouds of gas and dust. Its variety comes partly from what the dust does to light. Thin dust can scatter starlight and glow blue, while thicker clouds hide background stars and leave dark lanes.

Elsewhere, ultraviolet radiation makes gas itself shine. The result is a field where brightness alone doesn't tell you whether you're seeing a star, dust reflecting light, or glowing gas. The globular cluster M4 lies in this wider patch of sky but is far behind the nearby cloud, not embedded in it.

images.label: NGC 6164 Dragon's Egg
images.distance_note: ~1.1 kpc (~3,600 ly) to the central star HD 148937 (Gaia DR3 offset-corrected parallax, cited Lim et al. 2024); older estimates 4,000–6,000 ly
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1834 (NGC 6164); the symmetric bipolar structure was recognised by Karl Henize, 1959. Conventional credit for NGC 6164: J. Herschel
images.description:
The Dragon’s Egg is the emission nebula NGC 6164/6165 in Norma. Its two lobes give it a roughly hourglass-like shape, centred on the massive stellar pair HD 148937. The gas is material expelled from the system, not the remains of a star that went supernova.

Observations suggest that there were once three stars and that two merged, leaving today’s pair and throwing off the gas now seen as the nebula. That is a leading explanation rather than a direct observation of the event. The lobes are the visible clues to a much less obvious history.

images.label: LDN 43 Cosmic Bat
images.distance_note: ~1,400 ly (~430 pc; APOD, Constellation Guide). [UNVERIFIED against a primary source — some studies of associated young stars (RNO 90/91) imply a nearer ~125–140 pc; the two figures are in tension. Constellation confirmed as Ophiuchus from the coordinates]
images.discovered_by: Beverly T. Lynds, 1962 (Lynds Dark Nebulae catalogue). Conventional credit: Lynds
images.description:
The Cosmic Bat is a dark molecular cloud in Ophiuchus. Its silhouette is not a hole in the star field: dust in the foreground absorbs and scatters the light of stars behind it.

Less opaque stretches of the cloud let more of that light through, while nearby young stars illuminate some of the surrounding dust. The result is a useful contrast between dust seen in silhouette and dust seen by reflected light. The bat shape is a chance outline, but the materials are the raw ingredients of star formation.

images.label: NGC 6188 Fighting Dragons (SHO)
images.distance_note: ~1.3 kpc (~4,300 ly): Arnal et al. 2003; Ara OB1a ~1,320–1,380 pc (Humphreys). Consistent with popular ~4,000 ly
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1836 (Rim Nebula NGC 6188); the ionising cluster NGC 6193 was recorded by James Dunlop, 1826. Conventional credit for NGC 6188: J. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 6188 lies in Ara, along the boundary between a molecular cloud and gas lit by young stars in the Ara OB1 association. The rugged shapes that suggest fighting dragons are dense material seen against the brighter emission. Where less dense gas is eroded, stubborn ridges of dust and gas can be left standing.

The colours separate light from sulphur, hydrogen and oxygen, letting regions with different emission stand out rather than imitating the view through an eyepiece. Look for the changing edges of the dark ridges, where the bright gas makes their outlines easiest to follow.

images.label: NGC 6188 Fighting Dragons (HOO)
images.distance_note: ~1.3 kpc (~4,300 ly): Arnal et al. 2003; Ara OB1a ~1,320–1,380 pc
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1836 (Rim Nebula); cluster NGC 6193 by James Dunlop, 1826. Conventional credit for NGC 6188: J. Herschel
images.description:
The Fighting Dragons trace the edge of a dense cloud in Ara, where young stars are changing the material they formed from. Their light makes the gas on the exposed side glow, while the thicker parts of the cloud resist being worn away.

In this view, the light emitted by hydrogen and oxygen highlights different parts of the boundary. Follow the brighter rims and then the fainter glow beyond them. The dragons are shapes we recognise in the picture, but the sharp edges tell a real story about where starlight meets cold gas.

images.label: SL 17 Fenrir (Sandqvist 17)
images.distance_note: Distance via associated RCW 113/Gum 55 and Sco OB1: NGC 6231 ~1,640 pc (Sana et al. 2008) to Sco OB1 ~1,910 pc (Humphreys); range 5,300–6,200 ly, midpoint ~1,775 pc. Genuinely uncertain
images.discovered_by: Aage Sandqvist & Kjell Lindroos, 1976 (catalogued in Sandqvist 1977, from ESO(B) Schmidt plates)
images.description:
The wolf-like shape of Sandqvist 17 is a dark cloud in Scorpius, seen against the glow of the nebula RCW 113. Its outline is visible because cold dust in the foreground blocks the light of hydrogen gas farther away.

The darker parts are not empty patches of sky: they are places where the dust keeps us from seeing what lies behind it. Look for the contrast along the edge of the silhouette. It is the bright background, rather than light from the wolf itself, that lets us trace the shape.

images.label: IC 4628 Prawn Nebula
images.distance_note: ~1,640 pc (~5,350 ly) via NGC 6231/Sco OB1 (Sana et al. 2008); popular ~6,000 ly
images.discovered_by: E. E. Barnard, ~1900 (photographic); IC designation in Dreyer's Index Catalogue. Conventional credit: Barnard
images.description:
The Prawn Nebula is a sprawling cloud of glowing gas in Scorpius. Young, massive stars in its neighbourhood give off intense ultraviolet light, which energises the gas and makes it shine. Look for the thin rims and wisps against the broader glow.

They trace surfaces where that light meets uneven clumps of surrounding material. The nebula is large on the sky but faint across much of its area, so its shape is easier to see by following those edges than by looking for one clearly defined outline. The nickname hints at a shape rather than a sharp boundary.

images.label: IC 4633 and the Apus IFN
images.distance_note: IC 4633 itself; the integrated flux nebula in front of it lies only a few hundred light-years away, inside our own galaxy
images.discovered_by: DeLisle Stewart
images.description:
This view in Apus stacks two scenes along the same line of sight. IC 4633 is the spiral galaxy in the distance. The faint, smoky veil is much closer: dust in the Milky Way reflecting the combined light of many stars, rather than being lit by a brightly obvious star nearby.

Astronomers call this faint foreground an integrated flux nebula. A useful way to read the photograph is to look for the organised shape of the spiral against the less orderly dust. The two overlap from Earth, but the clouds aren’t part of the distant galaxy.

images.label: NGC 6334 Cat's Paw Nebula
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1837 (Cape of Good Hope survey)
images.distance_note: 1.34 kpc from VLBI water-maser parallax, Chibueze et al. 2014. Older literature commonly says 5,500 ly. NOT from the deep-research pass - verify.
images.description:
The Cat’s Paw in Scorpius is a large, active region of star formation. Its rounded patches resemble the pads of a paw, but each is a pocket of gas lit by ultraviolet light from young, massive stars. Dust between the patches absorbs some of the glow and hides many of the stars still forming inside the cloud.

A visible-light view therefore traces the glowing surfaces and the dark intervening material, rather than showing all the activity within. Infrared observations can see through more of that dust and reveal young stars that would otherwise go unnoticed.

images.label: NGC 6357 Lobster Nebula
images.distance_note: ~1.7 kpc (~5,500 ly), professional Gaia/spectroscopic value (SIMBAD 1,800±140 pc; Russeil, Reid). The popular ~8,000 ly (2.4 kpc) is overstated
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1837 (Cape). Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 6357 is a sprawling nursery for young stars in Scorpius. One of its clusters, Pismis 24, contains unusually massive stars whose ultraviolet light makes surrounding gas glow. Their winds and radiation can clear hollows while denser pockets of gas and dust survive as ridges and pillars.

That juxtaposition gives the Lobster Nebula its jagged, almost carved appearance. A sharp boundary can mark the surface of a cloud being lit and worn away, rather than an abrupt end to the cloud itself. Beyond those bright edges, dust can still hide stars in the process of forming.

images.label: M20 Trifid Nebula
images.distance_note: ~1,180 pc (~3,850 ly), Kuhn et al. 2019/2021 (Gaia); older estimates 1.67 kpc and the 4,100–5,200 ly range are now superseded by Gaia astrometry
images.discovered_by: Charles Messier, 1764 (catalogued as M20; = NGC 6514). Conventional credit: Messier
images.description:
The Trifid Nebula in Sagittarius shows three different ways gas and dust interact with starlight. Hydrogen gives off light where hot young stars ionise it. Elsewhere, dust scatters starlight and can produce a blue reflection glow.

Thicker dust blocks light instead, making the dark lanes that divide the bright nebula into the three sections behind its name. Those lanes are not gaps in the cloud; they are some of its more opaque parts. The contrast between light made by gas, light reflected by dust and light hidden by dust is what makes M20 so distinctive.

images.label: M8 Lagoon Nebula
images.distance_note: ~1,250 pc (~4,080 ly), Damiani et al. 2017 (Gaia distance to the embedded cluster NGC 6530); consistent with the current guess
images.discovered_by: Cluster NGC 6530 noted by John Flamsteed c.1680; nebula recorded by Giovanni Hodierna before 1654 and catalogued by Charles Messier, 1764 (M8). Conventional credit: Messier
images.description:
The Lagoon Nebula is a vast stellar nursery in Sagittarius. The dark streak that gives it its name is a lane of dust seen against brighter gas. Much of that gas glows because ultraviolet light from young, hot stars strips electrons from hydrogen; light is released as the electrons recombine.

Look for the contrast between broad luminous clouds and small, sharply outlined knots. Some of the darkest knots are dense globules that can shelter very young stars. Near the intense central region, the hot star Herschel 36 lights the feature known as the Hourglass.

images.label: M8 Lagoon to NGC 6559 Chinese Dragon (wide)
images.discovered_by: M8: Giovanni Battista Hodierna, before 1654. NGC 6559: John Herschel, 1837
images.distance_note: ~1,250 pc, Damiani et al. 2017 (Gaia). Matches the separate M8 and NGC 6559 entries - one physical complex.
images.description:
The Lagoon Nebula and the much smaller NGC 6559 share a crowded stretch of the Milky Way in Sagittarius. The Lagoon is a large region of glowing hydrogen, crossed by dust that blocks the light behind it. NGC 6559 offers a more compact mix: some gas emits its own light, while nearby dust scatters starlight.

A wide view makes it easier to compare those luminous patches with the dark lanes among them. The abundance of stars comes from looking along the Milky Way towards its centre, not from all the stars belonging to the same cloud.

images.label: NGC 6559 Chinese Dragon
images.distance_note: ~1,250 pc (~4,080 ly), physically part of the M8/Lagoon complex (Gaia); popular ~5,000 ly. Range 4,100–5,000 ly
images.discovered_by: John Herschel, 1837 (Cape). Conventional credit: J. Herschel
images.description:
In NGC 6559, east of the Lagoon Nebula, different materials leave three very different signatures. Hydrogen gas gives off reddish light after being energised by young stars. Dust scatters starlight to produce the softer blue patches.

The thickest dust appears dark because it blocks light from behind. Follow the winding bands where the three meet and you can see why the field earned the name Chinese Dragon. It is not one object with a neatly defined outline, but a small piece of a much larger region of gas, dust and young stars in Sagittarius.

images.label: Sh2-68 Flaming Skull
images.distance_note: PN G030.6+06.2. Distance poorly constrained; published values span roughly 1,000-2,300 ly
images.discovered_by: Stewart Sharpless
images.description:
The Flaming Skull is the remains of a Sun-like star in Serpens. Near the end of its life, the star shed its outer layers and left behind a white dwarf, the small, hot core that still lights the gas around it. These shells often look round, but this one has been pulled out of shape.

The star is travelling through the thin gas between stars. The two kinds of material push against each other, leaving the cloud lopsided rather than neatly centred. Its faint rim and ragged interior are reminders that the space around a star is not quite empty.

images.label: NGC 6726 Anteater / R CrA
images.distance_note: 149 pc (~486 ly), Galli et al. 2020 (Gaia DR2); Zucker et al. 2020 151 pc. Supersedes the older ~130 pc (425 ly) kinematic value
images.discovered_by: Johann F. J. Schmidt, 1861 (NGC 6726/6727). Conventional credit: Schmidt
images.description:
The Corona Australis cloud is one of the nearest regions where stars are forming. In this part of the cloud, the bluish reflection nebula NGC 6726 shines by dust scattering starlight, rather than by hot gas producing light of its own.

Dark streaks show where thicker dust hides the background stars. Another nebula in the same region, NGC 6729, is associated with the variable young star R Coronae Australis. The area is a good example of how the same dust can look bright near a light source and dark when seen against distant stars.

images.label: NGC 6729 Corona Australis
images.distance_note: 149 pc (~486 ly), Galli et al. 2020 (Gaia DR2); Zucker et al. 2020 151 pc
images.discovered_by: Johann F. J. Schmidt, 1861 (variable nebula); independently noted by Albert Marth, 1864. Conventional credit: Schmidt
images.description:
The dust clouds of Corona Australis look close together in this wide view, but the scene brings together very different distances. The glow around the young star R CrA is light scattered by nearby dust, part of a stellar nursery roughly 400 light-years away.

Follow the glow outwards and it gives way to darker strands, where dust blocks light from behind it. The globular cluster NGC 6723 lies far beyond the cloud. Its tightly packed stars happen to share the same patch of sky, not the same neighbourhood in space.

images.label: NGC 6744 Pavo Galaxy
images.distance_note: 9.01±0.38 Mpc (Anand et al. 2021, PHANGS-HST TRGB); NED redshift-independent mean ~7.2 Mpc. TRGB best regarded
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826 (Parramatta, NSW). Conventional credit: Dunlop
images.description:
NGC 6744 is a spiral galaxy in Pavo whose broad shape looks remarkably like the Milky Way. The bright centre gives way to loose arms dotted with regions where new stars are forming. It is a useful change of perspective: we see our own galaxy from inside its disc, but here we can follow the spiral pattern from the outside.

A small, distorted companion lies nearby. The pairing recalls the Milky Way and its Magellanic Clouds, even though the galaxies are not exact counterparts. NGC 6744 lies about 30 million light-years away.

images.label: NGC 6752
images.distance_note: About 13,000 light-years (commonly quoted; Boyles et al. 2011 give 4.0 kpc. Baumgardt & Vasiliev 2021 give about 13,500 ly).
images.discovered_by: James Dunlop, 1826
images.description: NGC 6752, the Great Peacock, is one of the brightest globular clusters in the sky, in Pavo, about 13,000 light-years away. More than 100,000 ancient stars are packed into a ball only about 100 light-years across, with a brilliant, tightly compressed core. James Dunlop found it in 1826 from Parramatta.

images.label: Eagle Ray Nebula
images.distance_note: Tentative ~215 pc (~700 ly) from association with a high-latitude molecular cloud in the Aquila Rift (Magnani et al. 1985). [UNVERIFIED — the identification with Sh2-63/LBN 82 and this distance could not be confirmed against a primary catalogue entry this session; treat as provisional]
images.discovered_by: Stewart Sharpless, 1959 (Sharpless catalogue, as Sh2-63/LBN 82). [Identification UNVERIFIED]
images.description:
The Eagle Ray Nebula, also catalogued as Sharpless 2-63, is a faint region against the crowded star fields of Sagittarius. The darker forms are interstellar dust seen against the light of more distant stars; where dust scatters nearby starlight rather than blocking it, it can show up as a softer glow.

Look at the change in the background as the shape emerges from the star field. The outline is subtle, and the contrast between crowded patches of stars and the dust that hides them helps make the ray-like form visible.

images.label: NGC 6888 Crescent Nebula
images.distance_note: Commonly quoted value (older estimates 1.26 to 1.45 kpc). Gaia puts WR 136 farther, about 1.9 kpc or 6,200 ly (Bailer-Jones et al. 2018)
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1792
images.description: The Crescent Nebula, NGC 6888, is a shell of glowing gas in the constellation Cygnus, about 4,500 light-years away and roughly 20 to 25 light-years across. A single star blew it: WR 136, a Wolf-Rayet star that began with 25 to 40 times the mass of the Sun and now throws off a wind at around 1,800 kilometres per second. That fast wind is ploughing into the slower wind the star shed earlier as a red supergiant, piling the gas into a shell, while shocks and the star's ultraviolet light make it glow. Chandra X-ray observations show gas inside the bubble heated to millions of degrees, and the nebula's nitrogen and oxygen carry the mark of material processed in the star's core. WR 136 is expected to end its life as a supernova. William Herschel found the nebula in 1792.

images.label: NGC 6960 Veil Nebula
images.distance_note: 725±15 pc (~2,360 ly), Fesen et al. 2021, MNRAS 507, 244 (Gaia EDR3 parallaxes of stars in/behind the Cygnus Loop). Verified
images.discovered_by: William Herschel, 1784. Conventional credit: W. Herschel
images.description:
NGC 6960 is the western part of the Veil Nebula, a vast remnant in Cygnus left by a star that exploded thousands of years ago. The blast wave is still travelling through surrounding gas. As shocked material cools, it radiates, making delicate-looking filaments that are very different from the long strands they resemble.

Many are thin sheets whose glow looks strongest where we see the folds edge-on. Other arcs, fainter or more broken, belong to the same expanding remnant. The full Cygnus Loop covers roughly six full-Moon diameters, so a close view shows just a piece of a much larger structure.

images.label: NGC 7293 Helix Nebula
images.distance_note: ~200 pc (655±13 ly), Gaia EDR3 parallax (~5.01 mas) of the central white dwarf WD 2226-210 (Gaia Collaboration 2021)
images.discovered_by: Karl Ludwig Harding, before 1824. Conventional credit: Harding
images.description:
The Helix Nebula is the glowing envelope shed by a dying Sun-like star. At its centre is a white dwarf, the exposed core, whose ultraviolet radiation still lights up the gas that the star lost. The bright rings and faint outer material can look like a flat bull's-eye, but they are different layers of a three-dimensional structure.

Dense pockets of gas in the inner region have tails pointing away from the central star. Known as cometary knots because of their shape, they show how some parts of the old stellar envelope survive longer as radiation and winds reshape it.

images.label: M33 Triangulum Galaxy
images.distance_note: About 3 million light-years (NASA Hubble Messier Catalog).
images.discovered_by: Charles Messier, 1764
images.description:
Triangulum is the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group, after Andromeda and the Milky Way. Its light takes about three million years to reach us. We see the disc nearly face-on, so you can follow its loose spiral arms away from the centre. Blue patches mark groups of young stars; pink knots are clouds of hydrogen glowing in their light.

Look just above and right of the centre for NGC 604, the brightest pink patch. This stellar nursery stretches nearly 1,500 light-years across. The young stars inside are not just lighting the cloud: their winds are carving cavities in it.
